newsitem.title: CYPRUS: British tourists sue soldiers for Cyprus assault.
newsitem.headline: British tourists sue soldiers for Cyprus assault.

text.p: Three Britons attacked in a Cyprus seaside resort earlier this month are suing five British soldiers accused of the assault for damages, their lawyer said on Monday.
"The civil law suit was filed this morning," said George Pittadjis. "My clients are suing for general, special and exemplary damages," he said.

Holidaymakers Shane Bell and Barry Ford, both 23, and Claire Harbour, 22, are each suing the five British soldiers accused of attacking them at the holiday resort of Ayia Napa for a joint sum of up to 25,000 Cyprus pounds ($45,375).

Soldiers Roger Bell, 26, Tim Carter, 20, Steven Wolstencroft, 26, Steven Girvan, 20, and Stuart Spencer, 20, also face state prosecution on charges of causing grievous and actual bodily harm to the three tourists.They have pleaded not guilty.
Shane Bell's jaw was fractured and Barry Ford's wrist broken in the early-morning attack outside a nightclub.
Shane Bell and Roger Bell are not related.
The Famagusta district court, sitting in Larnaca, on Monday ordered a further postponement to the start of the trial for Thursday after the lawyer for the five defendants withdrew.

Lawyer Kyriakos Kourtis cited "legal problems" in undertaking the case, without giving further details. Tassos Katsikides, a well-known local criminal lawyer, has taken over the defence of Roger Bell and Stuart Spencer. The other three are expected to appoint lawyers by the next court hearing.
At Katsikides's request the court cancelled a 2,000 Cyprus pounds bond imposed previously and released the soldiers into the custody of the British bases authorities.
The accused are riflemen with the 600-strong Kings Regiment based at the British base of Dhekelia.
The attack prompted the British base authorities to impose a ban on visits to Ayia Napa by members of the Kings regiment, just one month after another ban on soldiers' visits to the area was lifted.

The restrictions were first imposed in September 1994 after the brutal killing of a Danish tour guide by three members of the Royal Greenjackets regiment. They are now serving a life sentence in Cyprus's central prison.
Around 3,500 British troops are stationed at two military bases Britain has retained in Cyprus since independence in 1960. ($=0.55 pounds)
